sentences.text: Future enhancement of the Regional Flow Platform should be treated as an incremental extension of the operational service rather than as a replacement of the current concept.
The first expansion path is the exchange of cross-border flow constraints, demand forecasts, and agreed measures with adjacent regional systems under defined governance arrangements.
This capability would allow the Regional Flow Manager and Network Operations Liaison to see upstream demand pressure earlier and to negotiate measures before local capacity is saturated.
Cross-border exchange should use standardized message structures where practical, but the Business Rules Registry should retain the local parameters needed for Meridian operations.
The Flight Data Exchange should be enhanced to accept richer intent data, including improved route options, expected cruise profiles, and updated departure readiness information.
The Demand Prediction Service should use this data to create more stable demand pictures across longer planning horizons while still preserving tactical responsiveness.
Trajectory prediction should also make greater use of weather features, sector configuration, runway direction, and surface movement status when estimating flight progress.
The Weather Ingest Gateway and Sector Load Monitor should provide the common inputs needed to connect airspace capacity and airport capacity in the same prediction cycle.
The Capacity Assessment Module should evolve from a mainly rules-based assessment into a service that can compare planned capacity, observed throughput, and predicted constraint persistence.
Any use of learning models should be introduced with explainability requirements so that operational users can understand why a capacity or delay estimate has changed.
Advanced turnaround prediction should combine aircraft state, handling milestones, stand occupancy, crew readiness, passenger processing, and ramp congestion signals.
The Airport CDM Portal, Airline Interface Adapter, Handling Resource Planner, and Ramp Movement Board should provide the main operational inputs for this capability.
Predicted changes to Target Off Block Time should be presented with confidence levels rather than as unconditional system corrections.
The Slot Allocation Engine should use improved turnaround predictions to protect feasible Calculated Takeoff Time assignments and to reduce avoidable re-sequencing.
The Tower Sequence Manager and Departure Metering Service should receive only the information needed for tactical sequencing, with detailed airline operational data controlled by policy.
Machine-assisted recovery options should support the Recovery Phase by proposing coordinated actions that balance runway throughput, sector loading, stand availability, and airline priorities.
These options should be generated by the Contingency Operations Console and reviewed through the Common Situation Display before any operational decision is applied.
The system should not automatically impose a Ground Delay Program, change an Airport Acceptance Rate, or alter a tactical measure without authorized human confirmation.
Recovery recommendations should include the operational rationale, expected benefit, key assumptions, and possible secondary effects on connected flights and surface movements.
The Collaborative Decision Log and Audit Event Ledger should record each proposed option, the user response, and the final decision so that performance can be reviewed after operations.
Regional expansion should include a repeatable onboarding pattern for new airports, airspace sectors, airlines, and handling organizations.
The Identity Access Service, Time Synchronization Service, and Performance Analytics Warehouse should be scaled early because they form shared foundations for a wider regional deployment.
Data governance should remain under the Data Governance Steward, with clear rules for retention, consent, quality thresholds, and permitted operational use.

Future releases should be validated in shadow mode before operational activation so that the Regional Flow Manager, Airline Operations Coordinator, Tower Supervisor, and Airport Duty Manager can compare recommendations with actual outcomes.
